news.title: Book Excerpt: Unravelling snow leopard mysteries in ‘The Ghost of the Mountains’ by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi - The Tribune
news.text: The snow leopard has become a modern symbol for romantic ideals, yet the snow leopards are rarely ever truly away from people. Research on the snow leopard diet shows that a large proportion comprises livestock. Some biologists argue that livestock is essential for or subsidises snow leopard conservation. In contrast, my research has shown that while snow leopards eat a fair amount of livestock, their populations increase only with the availability of wild herbivore prey.Örjan Johansson’s research using satellite collars has shown that less than 10 per cent of protected areas in the high regions are large enough to have a viable population of fifteen or more snow leopards. And most of these protected areas are not free of humans. They contain a large number of villages that have been around for hundreds if not thousands of years.The parks, largely set up between the 1970s and the 2000s, were often designated as protected land without consideration of the existing human population. The pastoralists who lived in the high mountains were invisible to the administration.Only a handful of snow leopard habitats are truly without any people. The Nanda Devi National Park in Uttarakhand has 250 square kilometres of inner sanctum which is untouched except for an occasional mountaineering expedition. Although this is one of the most coveted regions for climbers, the Indian government is restrictive in giving permission for mountaineers to visit. The rumour is that the government collaborated with the American CIA in the 1970s to set up a device on the summit of Nanda Devi, the highest peak in the region, to spy on Chinese nuclear and missile-testing work across the border in the north.The inner region is surrounded by high peaks and ridges, some reaching over 7,000 metres. The only access is along the Rishiganga gorge, with the Trisul (7,120m) and Dunagiri (7,066m) peaks on either side. The sides of this gorge are treacherous.I had my eyes set on something even bigger. The Sarychat-Ertash Nature Reserve in the Tien Shan mountains of Kyrgyzstan is a contiguous stretch of 1,500 square kilometres of snow leopard habitat that has no other form of human use, at least not currently.By early 2017, I had been the Director of the India programme of the Snow Leopard Trust for two years. The Trust had a small programme in Kyrgyzstan. I had already set up multiple projects to monitor populations of blue sheep, ibex and argali in parts of India and Mongolia.I had many questions about Sarychat, such as how many snow leopards live there? What densities do ibex and argali achieve in the absence of competition from livestock? And what is the snow leopard’s diet in a place where there is no livestock? Sarychat was my best bet to study the population density of snow leopards and their prey before humans arrived on the scene.Kubanychbek Jumabay-Uulu, known to us as Kuban, the Director of the Kyrgyz programme of the Snow Leopard Trust, was already doing research in Sarychat-Ertash Nature Reserve. He had been deploying cameras to identify the snow leopards that live there. What Kuban had not yet done was estimate the prey populations.My aim is to make conservation recommendations that allow for human and non-human species to live together with as little cost to each other as possible. But the scientist in me was curious to understand what the highest densities of wild herbivores and snow leopard would be if they were given a chance away from humans.I was also hoping to see a snow leopard. By now, I had seen them more than fifteen times, but this was not about racking up the tally mark — I would never leave Spiti if I wanted to simply increase my count.As well as estimating the population of argali and ibex, we would also research populations in the adjacent hunting reserve. The Koilu hunting concession was used for cattle grazing as well as grounds for sports hunters to shoot big trophies of ibex and argali. In 2017, a single licence to shoot an ibex cost upwards of $2,000 USD and an argali over $20,000 USD.Collecting animal trophies may be as old as humans, but this is a poor justification for the current practice. The rarer the species, the higher the demand, and the licence fees. This leads to an incentive to keep a species rare because it brings in greater fees.A single licence to hunt a markhor goat in Pakistan costs more than $100,000. This programme is often cited as a success story as a large share of the licence money is shared with the local community. However, critics allege that hunting incentivises illegal persecution of snow leopards and wolves because the carnivores deplete the population of markhor, which make up a part of their diets.In the 2010s, an ignominious researcher had secured permission from the Mongolian government to ‘put down’ four snow leopards to study their reproductive biology. The perverse idea was to have wealthy hunters bid for the right to hunt these four poor snow leopards. The global scientific and conservation community was unanimous in pressuring the Mongolian government to withdraw the permission.The snow leopard is the only species of big cat that has never been the object of trophy hunting. Their small size and lack of aggression towards humans has always made them an unworthy opponent to those hunters who wanted to pit themselves against the might of the Big Five of Africa, the Indian tiger or the impressively horned Himalayan mountain goats and sheep.— Excerpted with permission from Penguin Random House

news.title: New penguin species named for first time in over 100 years
news.text:
According to the researchers, the different species developed over the past 300,000 to 500,000 years. 

Gentoos differ from other penguin species mainly due to their wide-ranging diet, and will eat almost anything they can catch in the water. 

This makes it easier for them to survive than penguins like emperors and Adelies, with more specific diets, who can struggle to find food.

Scientists argue that this is why gentoos evolved differently. 

Because they don't travel far from their breeding colony, and nest in the same place year after year, different populations developed who adapted to their specific regions.
news.summary: Southeastern gentoo penguin look almost identical to other gentoo penguins, so until recently experts thought they were all the same species.

news.title: Scientists discover new penguin species through breakthrough genetic analysis
news.text: THE TAKEAWAY Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, discovered a new species of gentoo penguin, the southeastern gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis kerguelensis), after reviewing genetic evidence from the animal. What was once considered a single, wildly different species has now opened the door to classifying three other gentoo penguins, rather than one species. It is easy to pass off this penguin as just another gentoo because of its white underside and black back, which are vital for escaping predators and hunting prey. There are slight differences in size and vocalization, but it is genetically distinct and what scientists call a cryptic species. Gentoo penguins differ from most others because they eat basically anything they can get their fins on in the water. NEW WILD CAT SPECIES DISCOVERED AFTER HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT FOR MORE THAN A CENTURY Researchers argue that the gentoo evolved into this type of new species as a result of their generalized diet including fish, krill, squid and cuttlefish, not needing to travel far from their habitats as they nest in the same place every year. This ideal and isolated environment that this species of penguin has inhabited for the last 300,000 to 500,000 years on the remote islands by the Antarctic Polar front has directly contributed to its development into an entirely new species over time. For the last 100 years, researchers have gone back and forth on how many species or subspecies of penguin there are, but genome data now enables a new, cutting-edge integrative approach to answer these questions. MEET THE 1-IN-100 MILLION ‘GHOST’ LOBSTER HELPING SCIENTISTS UNLOCK A COLORFUL MYSTERY The genomic analysis, led by University of Chile graduate student Daly Noll, revealed how these species evolved to adapt to their environments. For example, genes in the southern gentoo penguin allowed the species to adapt to the extreme polar environment over time, with more genes shifting toward heat generation, fat and lipid storage, and light perception. SEE IT: RARE TWO-HEADED TURTLE HATCHLING FOUND ON CAPE COD With further cutting-edge technology, scientists may discover other subspecies variations and possibly entirely new ones, like the southeastern gentoo penguin.
news.summary: Scientists have made a brand-new discovery of a penguin species after genetic analysis revealed an entirely new category of the animal.

news.title: At the bookend of summer, here are September’s best reads
news.text:
These are the fiction titles our reviewers liked best this month.

The Birthing Tree, by Amanda Peters (Penguin Random House)

Thirty-something city dweller Aliet – raised by her midwife grandmother Kiju and their extended Mi’kmaw community – returns to rural Nova Scotia after learning of Kiju’s passing. Inheritances, both official and intangible, await: the now-ramshackle cabin, well-worn recipes, as well as Kiju’s despair over the government-enforced abandonment of traditional birthing practices. As Aliet rebuilds the property and faces her own aches – a mother who died giving birth to her, an unknown father, a relationship cut short – she finds strength and new purpose. It’s a warmhearted story that embraces the bumpy, invigorating path of preservation and repair. – Erin Douglass

Exit Party, by Emily St. John Mandel (Penguin Random House)

Emily St. John Mandel’s speculative tale, rejecting the proverbial “road not taken,” posits a world in which characters can indeed travel two diverging paths. Here, differing future visions of the United States unfurl: one authoritarian and monolithic, surveilling, subduing, and corralling its citizens; the other fractured, with militias, city-states, and pockets of fragile calm. Ari Waker, fresh out of prison and living in Los Angeles circa 2031, realizes something is amiss when she attends a party where someone disappears and someone else ... seems to be in two places. Mysterious, somber, or maybe just sober, the book has a thoughtful, shivery vibe. – Erin Douglass

The Pirate Queen, by Ariel Lawhon (Penguin Random House)

Clear the decks – or at least find a long weekend – for Ariel Lawhon’s historical adventure. A fictional imagining of the very real 16th-century Irish sailor, leader, and liberator Grace O’Malley, this rip-roaring tale interweaves the three chapters of her never-dull life: maiden, mother, and matriarch. Lawhon does her research and has a ball with her characters. Full of big feeling and brisk banter, it’s another winner from the bestselling author. – Erin Douglass

The Oxford Guide to Scandal & Lies, by Kate Westbury (Minotaur Books)

This rollicking historical mystery presents two collegians hired by British Intelligence to ferret out a Soviet spy responsible for poisoning an MI5 agent at Oxford University. Debutante Ginevra Bishop enthusiastically matches wits with pensive ex-soldierSidney Braithwaite, both deftly sidestepping romantic attraction. They dodge danger and swap banter while attempting to unknot the tangle of possible culprits. The novel delivers high-spirited fun with charm to spare. – Stefanie Milligan

American Hagwon, by Min Jin Lee (Cardinal)

Min Jin Lee digs into work – the work of learning, the toil of earning, and the persistent effort of immigrants navigating unfamiliar landscapes and altered expectations. But “American Hagwon” is no chore. This richly told, wise book is also a blast to read. The successful Koh family of five, with roots in Australia, the United States, and South Korea, leaves Sydney for Seoul. In mere months, a shocking event sets the father, John, reeling and their finances tumbling. Committing to a new start in Orange County, California, in the midst of the late ’90s Asian financial crisis, the family members transform. Page after page illuminates innovation, loyalty, and steadfastness, yet Min Jin Lee saves her strongest grilling for education itself: Is it a means to material wealth? A pressure cooker for children? A tool for self-knowledge? It’s an enormous, embracing book well worth the time. – Erin Douglass

We’re So Lucky to Live Here, by Rachel Pastan (Delphinium Books)

Rachel Pastan’s life-affirming novel revolves around young Pittsburgh theater director Gwen Rivlin’s journey through grief. After her mother’s death, Gwen returns to the rambling, turreted house where she grew up. She discovers that her mother took out a second mortgage, so the property might be unaffordable for Gwen to keep. She takes in an assortment of housemates, who help her stage a production of Anton Chekhov’s “The Cherry Orchard” inside the home. The themes of chosen family and the power of creativity to conquer grief are threaded through Pastan’s story. – Stefanie Milligan

Sisters of the Midnight Sun, by Fiona Valpy (Penguin Random House)

On the Shetland Islands in northern Scotland in 2001, an older woman, Hanna, and her younger companion, Ruby, find sanctuary in friendship. Each is grieving a lost twin sister. One woman’s twin died long ago; the other’s died more recently. This dual-timeline World War II historical novel highlights Norwegian resistance against the Nazi occupation, as well as the existence of light and delight in the darkest times. For both women, discovering a kindred spirit and embracing hope inspires strength and renewal. – Stefanie Milligan

Ply, by Hernan Diaz (Penguin Random House)

Set in a post-apocalyptic future, a young woman survives as a “pincher,” someone who steals electricity off the power grid to sell on the black market. Her work is dangerous, but it immerses her in the nascent music scene as she powers underground concerts, revealing that societal institutions might have collapsed, but the arts have endured. With insight and artistry, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Hernan Diaz explores a futuristic society and the evolving place of technology. Even readers who usually don’t care for sci-fi or futuristic plots might find themselves enjoying this novel. – Joan Gaylord

These are the nonfiction titles our reviewers liked best this month.

Receipts From the Bookshop, by Katie Clapham (Harper Collins)

In the spirit of Shaun Bythell’s “The Diary of a Bookseller,” Katie Clapham takes us through a year in the life of the bookstore she and her mother operate in coastal England. Clapham’s stiff upper lip in the face of sometimes comical travails is quintessentially British, as is this narrative’s wet and windy setting. For readers who will never visit Clapham’s shop in person, this diary is perhaps the next best thing to being there. – Danny Heitman

The Butterfly Season, by Lea Korsgaard (Penguin Random House)

Danish journalist Lea Korsgaard’s lovely, inspirational book documents her self-imposed challenge to see all of Denmark’s 64 butterfly species in a single year. The result is much more than an account of her search for the elusive, increasingly rare lepidoptera. Korsgaard spreads her wings in “The Butterfly Season” to encompass an overview of butterflies in history, art, and literature along with a meditation on beauty, transformation, and spirituality. – Heller McAlpin

True North: On the Road in Canada, by Paul Theroux (Harper Collins)

“True North” is Paul Theroux’s expansive, topical, and sympathetic account of the many months he spent driving thousands of miles in Canada. His French-born ancestor, Antoine Theroux, landed in Quebec City in 1693 as a teenage military recruit to defend New France for King Louis XIV. Centuries later, Theroux asks farmers, truckers, wait staff, fellow diners, writers, and bystanders – many of them immigrants and Indigenous people – about what it is to be Canadian, and their opinions of U.S.-Canada relations. – Heller McAlpin

Voice of a Century: The Life and Artistry of Marian Anderson, by Anthony Tommasini (Penguin Random House)

Marian Anderson is best known for her triumphant 1939 concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, organized after the Black contralto was barred from performing at the city’s Constitution Hall. In his illuminating biography, Anthony Tommasini covers both Anderson’s groundbreaking accomplishments and the racial discrimination she confronted throughout her career. Most notably, the author, former chief classical music critic for The New York Times, crafts an insightful and authoritative appreciation of Anderson as a musical artist. – Barbara Spindel

Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea: Journeys Through Ancient Literature, by Emily Wilson (W.W. Norton)

The essays in classicist and translator Emily Wilson’s new book provide an absorbing investigation into the art of translation and the pleasures of reading the classics. Noting that the ancient and modern worlds intersect, Wilson brings in Leonard Cohen, Erica Jong, and Cardi B. to join the familiar figures from the past. Wilson analyzes various translations of “The Odyssey,” including her own, and includes a lengthy, fascinating exegesis on her translation of a single word in the opening line of the poem. – David Conrads
news.summary: Monitor reviewers recommend titles by Emily St. John Mandel, Min Jin Lee, and Paul Theroux.

news.title: Scientists identify new species of penguin in subantarctic waters — the first in over a century
news.text:
Scientists have discovered a brand-new species of penguin — marking the first newly named species of the aquatic bird in over a century.

Dubbed the southeastern gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis kerguelensis), the bird calls the subantarctic Kerguelen and Heard Islands in the southern Indian Ocean home.

It was formally recognized as a distinct species after an exhaustive genomic, morphological and ecological study led by an international team of researchers.

The team of 22 scientists — hailing from the US and Chile — published their landmark findings last April in the journal Communications Biology.

The southeastern gentoo looks identical to other gentoo penguins, which were grouped as one species for generations. 

However, the breakthrough study proves gentoos actually comprise four separate species: the northern gentoo (P. papua), southern gentoo (P. ellsworthi), eastern gentoo (P. taeniata), and southeastern gentoo (P. kerguelensis).

“There’s probably no species of penguin where the taxonomy has been more debated than the gentoo penguin,” said Rauri Bowie, a curator and professor at UC Berkeley’s Museum of Vertebrate Zoology.

“For over 100 years it’s been controversial as to how many species or how many subspecies there are. What this paper does is try to address that question using cutting-edge integrative approaches.”

Researchers contend that the gentoos’ flexible diet indirectly fueled their evolutionary split.

Because the birds gladly feast on whatever prey is nearby — including fish, krill, squid, and cuttlefish — they stick close to home and nest in the same spots year after year rather than migrating.

As a result, isolated island populations developed distinct behavioral and ecological habits that were locked in genetically over time.

Combined with geographical isolation and the ocean barrier of the Antarctic Polar Front, this lifestyle drove the creation of new species over the last 300,000 to 500,000 years, according to the team.
news.summary: For generations, gentoo penguins were classified as a single species.
news.author: Daniel Cody

news.title: As yellow-eyed penguins disappear, conservationists focus on deaths in fishing nets
news.text:
OTAGO PENINSULA, Aotearoa New Zealand — Sandfly Bay was long a key nesting area for yellow-eyed penguins (Megadyptes antipodes), noisy, pink-footed birds that spend long days foraging at sea. But this wild beach on the Otago Peninsula, like others nearby, has gone quiet. In 2024, the last breeding-age female at Sandfly Bay, who’d been consistently producing chicks for a dozen years, drowned in a fishing net.

Fishing has been one of many factors driving the species, which is only found in Aotearoa New Zealand, toward extinction. In the 2008-2009 breeding season, there were 739 breeding pairs in the “mainland” New Zealand population, which includes pairs on nearby islands. But the population has dropped since then to 117 pairs — a decline of more than 80%. These figures don’t account for yellow-eyed penguins on New Zealand’s remote southern islands, which are poorly surveyed.

The IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, listed the species as endangered in its last assessment, in 2020, when the mainland population was still twice what it is now. Several experts told Mongabay that the species’ chances of survival are slim, though most said they still had faith.

“I think I’d always like to say that there’s hope because otherwise why do you do what you do, but things are pretty dire,” Trudi Webster, a marine scientist who’s worked on research and conservation of the species for the past decade, told Mongabay.

A number of organizations are working to save the yellow-eyed penguin, and much of the conservation concern has centered on set-net fishing. Set nets act as a vertical wall anchored in the water that catches fish by their gills or entangles them. They’ve drowned numerous yellow-eyed penguins. Over the objections of fishers, the New Zealand government recently opted to make a set-net closure around the Otago Peninsula permanent and set an annual fishing-related mortality limit of four penguins. Conservationists say it’s not enough.

A treasured species, a multitude of threats

Yellow-eyed penguins are an iconic species in New Zealand, appearing on the $5 bill and drawing tourists to Otago. Stuffed yellow-eyed penguins even greet travelers at the airport in Dunedin, the area’s main city.

The species is often called hoiho, a Māori name meaning “noise shouter.” For Kāi Tahu, the Māori tribe whose traditional territory includes the southeast of the South Island, hoiho is a taoka, or treasured species, with deep cultural significance. The penguins are “navigators [that] arrived in a similar way to ourselves,” Hoani Langsbury, a prominent local conservationist and member of Te Rūnanga o Ōtākou, a branch of Kāi Tahu, told Mongabay.

“We have an affinity with those species that have managed to travel to our coastline and then adapt and stay here for a long period of time,” said Langsbury, who’s a trustee with the local nonprofit Yellow-Eyed Penguin Trust, among other roles. He added that it was sad “that our children that come after us are probably never going to even know those species were here,” referring to hoiho.

Scientists have traditionally divided yellow-eyed penguins into two populations: the mainland or, more officially, “northern” population that, confusingly, lives primarily on New Zealand’s South Island, and the “southern” population that lives on remote islands farther south.

The southern population, comprised of penguins at the Auckland Islands and Campbell Island, diverged from the mainland thousands of years ago. There seem to be more penguins there than in the mainland population, but the population hasn’t been studied recently. Genomic research published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution in May found that the penguins actually comprise three distinct lineages — mainland, Auckland and Campbell — and proposed recognizing each as a separate subspecies.

The penguins face a wide array of threats. These include predation by non-native land animals such as dogs, cats, weasels and rats. Langsbury, for his part, helped steer a massive yearslong project to eradicate possums, long ago introduced for their fur, from 10,000 hectares (roughly 25,000 acres) of the Otago Peninsula, which was completed in March. That effort wasn’t aimed solely at helping penguins, but efforts to reduce terrestrial pressures on them have been far-reaching at many nesting sites. Penguin Rescue, for example, is a local nonprofit that manages a large share of the remaining mainland population at three nesting sites near the town of Moeraki. The organization traps predators and maintains fencing to protect penguins from them and from human disturbance.

Two diseases have plagued mainland yellow-eyed penguin chicks in recent decades. One is diphtheritic stomatitis, first identified in 2002, which causes lesions and plaques in chicks’ mouths that can prevent them from eating and breathing. The other is respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), which was first identified in 2019 and causes severe breathing difficulties, killing more than 90% of chicks that catch it. And enough catch it that it’s a serious problem: RDS has been killing 25-40% of mainland chicks since 2021, according to Janelle Wierenga, head of wildlife management at the Otago Peninsula Eco Restoration Alliance (OPERA), a private reserve that includes a penguin rescue center. The hemorrhaging in the lungs can make it look like they’re filled with blood in necropsies, Wierenga said. The diseases aren’t known to affect the southern population, she said.

Penguin Rescue and the OPERA are part of a loose network of organizations that manage the species on the ground. So is Wildlife Hospital Dunedin, which, among other roles, treats or monitors nearly every mainland chick for both diseases.

“It’s still quite intensive management,” Wierenga told Mongabay, saying it was necessary to keep mortality rates down.

Caught in a set of debates

If it’s hard for conservationists to control what yellow-eyed penguins experience on land, the marine environment presents its own challenges. For one, their diet has in recent decades shifted away from juvenile red cod (Pseudophycis bachus), which has become less available due to warming seas and fishing pressure, and toward larger blue cod (Parapercis colias), which can be difficult for adults to regurgitate to their chicks.

Yet the marine issue that scientists and conservationists wanted to speak to Mongabay about was a threat they do see as preventable: set-net fishing, a form of gillnet fishing that is often called set gillnetting outside of New Zealand. (Set nets are anchored in place; other kinds of gillnets can drift.) Gillnets can be selective by size but are “not very species selective,” according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization. This means they pose a significant bycatch risk.

Since October 2019, 18 mainland yellow-eyed penguins have died in set nets, according to Fisheries New Zealand (FNZ), the government regulator. The real toll could be higher, as not all incidents are necessarily reported, though FNZ has had onboard cameras on all set net vessels in the southeast since October 2023 that incentivize fishers to report all unintended catch.

Experts said relatively few mainland chicks successfully run the gauntlet of threats they face on land and fledge into the marine environment, so when those that do are then killed by fishing gear, it’s particularly damaging to the population. Webster, the marine scientist, said the bycatch numbers might not look like much but when you consider how low the population numbers are, they are “actually a big problem.”

Ursula Ellenberg, a teaching fellow at the University of Otago Department of Marine Science, said this was the threat that could most directly be addressed through policy change.

“We can stop killing them in set nets tomorrow,” Ellenberg told Mongabay.

FNZ has taken action. In September 2025, it instituted a temporary ban on set-net fishing out to about 8 nautical miles (14.8 kilometers) from the shore around the Otago Peninsula; this ultimately stayed in effect for a year. (A prohibition on set-net fishing within 4 nm (7.4 km) of the shore already existed to protect endangered Hector’s dolphins (Cephalorhynchus hectori).) On Sept. 16, 2026, the 8nm closure became permanent, following a July announcement. Separate new rules that will take effect Oct.1 set an annual fishing-related mortality limit of four yellow-eyed penguins. This comes with an “escalating response framework” enabling FNZ to take progressively stronger action each time there’s yellow-eyed penguin bycatch. However, the rules don’t include an automatic fishery closure if the limit of four is exceeded.

Chanel Gardner, a frequent spokesperson for the local fishing industry and a director of Harbour Fish, one of the area’s main seafood businesses, told Mongabay that the temporary ban had already caused one family to stop fishing, taking a vessel out of the set-netting fleet. “It’s just super sad for everybody,” she said. Set-netting can “get painted with a very unfair brush when people don’t understand the local conditions,” she added.

She said the method is a targeted way to fish for rig (aka lemonfish, Mustelus lenticulatus), elephantfish (Callorhinchus milii) and school shark (Galeorhinus galeus), all used in fish and chips, a common and inexpensive meal in New Zealand.

Gardner said fishers go to the “nth degree” to protect yellow-eyed penguins and had called for a smaller, more targeted closure area. But their pleas “weren’t really given any weight because the emotional connotation of hoiho and that it’s so endangered and so precious really has overtaken the science and the pragmatism of it,” she said.

Gardner and other industry representatives have argued that yellow-eyed penguins wouldn’t recover even if set-net fishing ceased entirely. Conservationists dispute this interpretation and emphasize the importance of protecting individuals that have survived long enough to forage at sea and potentially breed.

Conservationists have themselves expressed frustrations with the new government rules, calling them inadequate. Forest & Bird, a prominent New Zealand conservation group, had pushed for a 14-nm (about 26-km) closure along the country’s entire southeastern seaboard; WWF-New Zealand made a similar proposal. Yellow-eyed penguins are known to travel as far as 27nm (50 km) offshore — or even further at Campbell Island — though they’re usually found within the range Forest & Bird proposed. Meanwhile, Otago is just one of several areas in the southeast that the penguins occupy; conservationists point out that there have been at least four set-net deaths near Rakiura (aka Stewart Island), one of the islands included in the mainland population, since 2021.

“The set net closure zone includes only a small part of the foraging range of hoiho,” Yolanda van Heezik, a zoology professor at the University of Otago, told Mongabay in an email.

“Given the parlous state of the population, losing 4 birds to the fishing industry per year is too many – if any one of them is a super-breeder, then it’s a catastrophe,” she added, referring to research that she co-authored showing that a small number of yellow-eyed penguins make a disproportionate contribution to future generations. In March, she co-authored an opinion piece in a local newspaper arguing that every breeding adult should be considered a potential super-breeder.

The Environmental Law Initiative, a New Zealand-based NGO, has argued that the escalation framework provides “little reassurance [because] there is no guarantee of a regulatory response, and if there was one, it would presumably only be in place for however long was left within the fishing year.”

Another threat?

In recent months, three birds found dead in New Zealand, none of them penguins, tested positive for H5N1 bird flu, raising concerns that an outbreak could affect more species including yellow-eyed penguins. Bird flu has caused penguin die-offs elsewhere in recent years; for example, at least 2,300 gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis papua) died of H5N1-related complications in the Falkland Islands in late 2024 and early 2025.

However, the last confirmed detection in New Zealand was on Aug. 21 and the three cases were outside the yellow-eyed penguins’ range. Moreover, yellow-eyed penguin nesting pairs are dispersed rather than packed into colonies, which could make them somewhat less vulnerable to bird flu than other penguin species, according to Ellenberg, the teaching fellow.

Ellenberg said the biggest threats to the species are longstanding, and she’s seen their effects firsthand. She shared the story of a male yellow-eyed penguin in the mid-to-late 2010s on Whenua Hou (aka Codfish Island), one of the islands included in the mainland population. He and his mate nested alongside old-growth forest, just beside a hut where Ellenberg would stay, and she would hear their loud “flirting” and banter with their chicks. Then the female disappeared. Yet the male couldn’t let go.

“For years he’d be there setting up, getting the nest ready, being ready for his partner to return, and every night he would walk down,” Ellenberg said, starting to cry and struggling to get her words out. “He would walk down to greet his partner at the beach. She would never come back, of course.”

9 Regional Ministers elected by the House of Assembly from among its members.

The power to propose the name of any person for election as a Regional Minister was vested in the Lieutenant-Governor. If his proposal was accepted, he then proceeded to appoint such a person as a Regional Minister. During the election, public officers who were members of’ the Legislative House concerned were disqualified from candidature, and precluded from voting. The President of the House had neither original nor casting votes at such an election.

The executive authority of Nigeria was vested in the Council of Ministers, the composition of which was as follows:

(1) The Governor who was President;

(2) 6 ex officio members of the House of Representatives;

(3) 4 Ministers elected by the Joint Council of the Northern Houses of Chiefs and assembly, from among the members of the House of Representatives representing the Northern Region, 1 of whom had to be a Chief;

(4) 4 Ministers elected by the Joint Council of the Western Houses of Chiefs and Assembly, in and of exactly the same manner and composition as in the North; and

(5) 4 Ministers elected by the Eastern House of Assembly from among the members of the House of Representatives representing the Eastern Region. As in the case of the Regions, the power to propose any person for election as Minister was vested in the Governor. If the proposal was accepted, then the person elected would be appointed by the Governor as a Minister.

It must be pointed out, at this juncture, that if the person proposed by either the Governor or the Lieutenant-Governor was rejected by the body responsible for electing him, then the Governor or the Lieutenant-Governor would have to propose another person.

Again, by virtue of Instructions passed under the Royal Sign Manual and the Signet, the Council of Ministers and the Regional Executive Council were only advisory to the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor respectively. And neither the Governor nor the Lieutenant-Governor was obliged to accept the advice of the Council of Ministers or the Executive Council, if he ‘considers it expedient in the interests of public faith, public order or good government that he should not act in accordance with such advice.

In spite of the Governor s and Lieutenant-Governor s tremendous powers there under, the Macpherson Constitution forms the watershed between British rule and indigenous administration in Nigeria.

We have noted the Governor’s and Lieutenant-Governor’s veto and reserved powers as well as Her Majesty’s power of disallowance, in relation to Bills and other legislative measures. We have also noted that the nomination of candidates for election as Central or Regional Ministers was the responsibility of the Governor or Lieutenant-Governor, and that the Council of Ministers or the Executive Council was merely advisory to the latter. In practice, however, these provisions of the constitution were virtually inoperative. Indeed, one of the major contributory causes of the premature demise of the Macpherson Constitution in 1954, was the determined attempt on the part of the Governor and his colleagues, to enforce these provisions.

From 1949 to 1950 when proposals for the Macpherson Constitution were considered and settled, there were no political parties with regional, let alone country-wide following and influence, in Nigeria. The only two political parties in the country confined their activities and membership chiefly to Lagos; and had, at the material time, sunk into a state of irretrievable decay. Consequently, the provisions of the constitution relating to Ministers had been framed in the firm belief, in British official circles, that a party system would not emerge in Nigeria until long after the introduction of the constitution. But Macpherson and his colleagues had miscalculated.

Shortly before the commencement of the series of elections under the new constitution, two virile political parties, with extensive region-wide-one of them with some country-wide-following and influence, had emerged. Each was determined to win the forthcoming elections in the Region or Regions of its base or where it could muster enough support, in order to form the new administration there. Attention was concentrated mainly in the Regions, first because they provided the ladder to the Centre, and secondly because it was there alone, as the constitution stood, that a party system could be made to work. After the elections, but before candidates were proposed for election as ministers, a third party of strong regional standing emerged.

The immediate effect of this sudden and unexpected emergence of a party system was twofold. In the first place, nearly all those ‘good’ men in the South who had been so much beloved by British officials, and on whom the latter had banked for co-operation in working the new constitution, had been defeated at the elections. The ‘good’ men of the North and the handful of them in the South, who had won the elections on their own individual merits, were impelled by sheer force of public opinion to become partisan politicians by teaming up openly with one or other of the new political parties. As a result, the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor were completely deprived of the services and support of their erstwhile faithful collaborators. In the second place, before they could attune their minds and adjust themselves to the novel situation, the Governor and the Lieutenant-Governors had been made, by irresistible pressure, to substitute the advice of political leaders for their own discretion, in the exercise of certain powers vested in them by the letters of the constitution. Consequently, they were obliged to nominate; as candidates for ministerial posts, names submitted to them by party leaders. They were also obliged to act in accordance with the advice of party leaders in the distribution of portfolios.

They simply had no choice in the matter. The only alternative open to them was to risk the humiliation and hostility of their nominees being rejected, in a declamatory manner, as was once the case in the Western Region. In that case, the nominated candidates not only criticized the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor for their reckless assault on the spirit of the constitution, but also proceeded along with their colleagues to vote against themselves.

Furthermore, the Regional Executive Council refused to play the role of advisers. They made it clear that they had been elected by their people to govern; and carried the day. Also, except on one or two occasions in the Eastern Region-that is, during a political crisis there – public opinion was mobilized to make the Governor and Lieutenant-Governors refrain from employing their veto and reserved powers. It must be pointed out that in addition to the force of public opinion, there was a good deal of in-fighting, behind the scenes, to ensure that the Governor or Lieutenant-Governor confined himself, in certain matters, to playing the role of a constitutional head. In other words, by intensive and sustained political actions, the role of the Governor or Lieutenant-Governor vis-a-vis his Ministers was reversed for all practical purposes: it was the former who was made to advise the latter, instead of the other way round as laid down in the constitution.

It must be emphasized that all these had not been achieved without . a good deal of friction and, sometimes, bad blood. But while Macpherson and his British colleagues seemed to think that an egregious mistake had been made by introducing a constitution, some of whose provisions turned out to be so easily amenable to political manoeuvres, the Nigerian nationalists were thankful and joyful The new constitution had afforded them a unique opportunity, and they were determined to exploit every loophole in it to wrest more and more powers from the British. No previous constitution had placed Nigerian nationalists in such an offensive and invulnerable vantage position. And it is true to say that Macpherson and his colleagues soon became utterly helpless and discomfited, in the face of the disconcerting assaults made on British rule in Nigeria through the powerful instrumentality of their own constitutional creation.

All these, by themselves, are quite enough to support the assertion that the Macpherson Constitution, and hence the year 1951, marks a clear, bold and indelible line of demarcation between British regime in Nigeria and Nigerian Home Rule. But there are other epoch-making features and events inseparable from the constitution, which are worth mentioning.

Firstly, with the introduction of the Macpherson Constitution, Nigeria took the first definite step on the road to federalism. In a strict scientific sense, the constitution itself can only be described as quasi-federal: residual powers were vested in the Central legislature; no Regional law could become operative without the prior approval of the Governor; and the House of Representatives as well as the Council of Ministers depended on the whims and caprices of the Regional legislatures for its Nigerian members. This dependence, in the case of the Council of Ministers, was so absolute that the political parties in the Regions could render it completely impotent.

In fact, a situation arose in 1953 which severely shook the Council of Ministers and threatened its existence. The Ministers from the Western Region, in obedience to a party directive, had resigned their seats in the Council, on the issue of a motion for self-government for Nigeria in 1956. With the absence of all the representatives of one of the three Regions from the Council, the legality of what remained of it became the subject of keen discussions both in Nigeria and the United Kingdom. In order to remedy the situation, the Governor decided to fill the vacancies. He and the remaining Nigerian Ministers did not like to have further association in the Council with two of the resigned Western Ministers. On the other hand, the party in power in the Western Region was adamant that the Region was not going to be represented by other than those four former Ministers who had surrendered their portfolios in the fight for Nigerian independence, and in unquestioning obedience to their party. Not daunted, the Governor nominated his four candidates; but they were rejected by the unanimous’ vote-taken by secret ballot-of the Joint Council. And so the deadlock remained. As time went on, however, he relented and decided to bow to the wishes of the party in power in the Western Region. But he was promptly confronted with the threat of resignation by the four Ministers from the Northern Region! Anyway, wiser counsels eventually prevailed, and the four former Ministers from the Western Region were nominated by the Governor and were duly re-elected to the Council of Ministers. This incident demonstrates beyond any equivocation the tightness and precariousness of Macpherson’s brand of quasi-federal constitution. It was obvious that some of its provisions had not taken account of certain kinds of human foible, temperament, and behaviour. And as we have said before, it had not envisaged the emergence of a disciplined party system. But even with all these grave defects, it remains true to say that the credit (or discredit, if; you like), for sowing the seeds of federalism in Nigerian administration belongs to the Macpherson Constitution.

Secondly, the ‘indirect rule’ system – a source of much irritation to Nigerian nationalists – died a natural death under the Macpherson Constitution. After Nigerians had assumed the reins of power, albeit ingeniously, it ceased to be practical politics for Traditional Rulers to look upon the Residents or Lieutenant- Governors as their principals in the business of public administration. In spite of themselves, they soon realized that, thenceforth, they had to depend on the goodwill of their people alone for a long, peaceful and successful reign. The vestiges of the Sole Native Authority system are still to be found in some parts of the Northern Region; but in spite of this, all Native Authorities (now known in the South as Local Governments) are now responsible to the people, through Nigerian Ministers.

Thirdly, partnership, in the true sense of the word, between the British and Nigerians in the administration of Nigeria, began only with the introduction of the Macpherson Constitution. British protestation of the existence of such a state of affairs, before 1952, was brazen hypocrisy, and false in the extreme. One might as well regard the office cleaner in a big business concern as a partner in the venture, simply because the undertaking had been organized to exploit natural resources exclusively belonging to the cleaner.

Fourthly, apart from the fact that Nigerian public men succeeded in playing the leading role in the management of their own affairs, the Nigerian taxpaying population, including women in some parts, for the first time had the welcome chance of choosing, though indirectly, their indigenous rulers and lawmakers. For 50 years previously, Nigerians were either passive onlookers, or negative critics, in the affairs of their land.

Fifthly, it was under the Macpherson Constitution that Nigerian leaders were afforded the much-needed and long-awaited opportunity for training in the art of modern government. For most Nigerian nationalists, their acquaintance with any form of public administration at all began with this constitution. Not being Chiefs, and having been daubed ‘agitators’ and ‘political adventurers’, they had up to then been largely excluded from taking part in public affairs – even in the affairs of the Native Authorities, in other words, the policy of preparing Nigerians for that day when Britain would ‘transfer to them the administration of all the governments’ was only allowed to unfold under the Macpherson Constitution.

Sixthly, the Macpherson Constitution was the involuntary precursor, through an unbroken and inexorable series of rapid constitution-making, of the Independence Constitution of 1960.

We have hinted before that the Macpherson Constitution came to a premature end in 1954. The author had hoped that it would last for many years. The generality of Nigerians themselves had expected that it should serve Nigeria for at least five years.

But this was not to be. The undue tightness of the constitution (which we have previously noted) together with some other circumstances, including the issue of self-government for Nigeria in 1956, brought about the breakdown of the constitution on 31 March 1953. Thereafter a chain of constitutional conferences began in 1953/54 and ended in 1957/58.

The 1953/54 Conference” introduced some radical constitutional changes:

I. A number of specified subjects were vested in the Federal Parliament, whilst the residuals were vested in the Regional legislature.

2. The House of Representatives was dissolved and reconstituted. Its Members from the East and West were directly elected, whilst those from the North were indirectly elected through provincial electoral colleges. The franchise in 1954 varied among the Regions. It was based on a tax-paying qualification in the West and North, which included females in certain parts of the West; whilst it was based on universal adult suffrage in the East and Lagos. Simultaneous membership of the Federal and Regional legislatures was abolished. (NOTE: Since 1956, the basis of franchise in the East, West, and Lagos has been universal adult suffrage. The North moved slightly further in 1957, to adult male suffrage, but this is retained to this day.)

3. Each Region had three Ministers in the Council of Ministers. But these Ministers were nominated, for appointment by the Governor, by the leader of the political party with a majority of members from that Region in the House of Representatives. There was also provision that if a political party had an overall majority of members in the House of Representatives, it would be entitled to nominate the Ministers from each Region.

4. The Government of each Region was headed by a Premier who was empowered to assemble, and apportion portfolios among, his team of Ministers.

5. The House of Representatives and the Council of Ministers no longer had official members as before, but continued to have three ex officio members as follows:

The Chief Secretary.

The Financial Secretary.

The Attorney-General.

The Governor, who now became Governor-General, continued to preside over the Council of Ministers.

6. With the exception of the Northern Region, the seats of all ex officio and official members in the Regional legislatures and Executive Councils were abolished. The Western Legislature was free to elect its own President (styled Speaker in the Western House of Assembly). The Governor (formerly Lieutenant-Governor) himself presided over the meetings of the Northern House of Chiefs; but the President of the Northern House of Assembly was appointed by the Governor acting in his discretion. In more or less the same fashion, the Speaker of the Eastern House of Assembly was appointed by the Governor acting in his discretion after consultation with the Leaders of the majority and Opposition parties.

7. The Governor of a Region (formerly Lieutenant-Governor) continued to preside over its Executive Council as before.

8. Under the Macpherson Constitution the Minister administered the Department (not Ministry) under his charge in association with the Official Head of the Department. What this meant in practice was that the Minister had no decisive say on any issue relating to his Department. If the Minister failed to carry the Official Head of the Department along on any subject, then the matter would have to fall into abeyance. This was one of the defects of the Macpherson Constitution. Accordingly, the new constitution conferred upon Ministers both at the Federal and Regional levels general direction and control of, and individual responsibility for, the Departments within their portfolios. Departments now became Ministries, and Official Heads of Departments became Permanent Secretaries of the Ministries.

9. Each Region had complete control of the personnel of the various sectors of its public service. But the appointment, promotion and discipline of Judges and Civil Servants remained vested in the Governor advised by a Public Service Commission.

10. Lagos was severed from the Western Region and declared a Federal Territory subject only to the authority of the Federal Government.

11. With regard to the demand for self-government in 1956, Her Majesty’s Government decided that it was not prepared to fix a definite date for self-government for Nigeria as a whole. However, it accepted a declaration of policy that it was prepared to grant, in 1956, ‘to those Regions which desired it, full self-government in respect of all matters within the competence of the Regional. Governments, with the proviso that there should be safeguards to ensure that the Regional Governments did not act so as to impede or prejudice the exercise by the Federal Government of the functions assigned to it now, or as amended by agreement in the future, or in any way make the continuance of the federation impossible. ‘5

12. The 1953/54 Conference agreed that another Conference should be convened not later than 31 August 1956, for the purpose of reviewing the new constitution, and examining the question of self-government. The last four words were later interpreted to mean the demand for a target date for self-government for the whole of Nigeria, as well as the detailed provisions for self-government by any Region which desired it. Her Majesty’s Government felt that it needed the long adjournment for three years to enable it to judge the capability of Nigerian leaders for additional political responsibility.

For reasons with which we do not need to concern ourselves here, the Conference did not reconvene until May 1957. At this Conference, both the East and the West were granted Regional Self-Government with effect from August 1957. It was at the resumed Conference of 1958 that Regional Self-Government was granted to the North with effect from March 1959. As a result of agreement reached at this Conference, a Nigerian Federal Head of Government, designated Prime Minister to distinguish him from Regional Premiers, was appointed in 1957.

A comprehensive review of the 1954 constitution which was initiated in 1957 was concluded at the resumed meetings of the Conference in 1958. It was at the close of this Conference that the famous declaration was made that ‘if a resolution is passed by the new Federal Parliament early in 1960 asking for independence, Her Majesty’s Government would agree to that request and would introduce a Bill in Parliament to enable Nigeria to become a fully independent country on the 1st October, 1960.’6 It must be pointed out that the detailed agreements reached at the 1957/58 Conference were embodied in Nigeria’s Independence Constitution of 1960. The legal drafting had taken about two years to accomplish.

It will be seen that it was from the ruins and ashes of the Macpherson Constitution that Nigeria’s swift and far-reaching political advances, beginning with a wide measure of Home Rule in 1954 and culminating in independence in 1960, had, like the mythical phoenix, arisen.
